After a conversation that started here the appropriately named @FriendlyCucco asked me to do an AMA about my time being homeless. So, here I am.

A little background about me:

I was born to two people who didn't love each other, and regularly had affairs. They got divorced when I was 2 years old, so all my memories are of them separate. They both remarried. My father, the same year to a very mentally unstable woman who happened to be amazing at committing fraud, and worked for the state at the time. And my mother remarried when I was 4 years old. Her new husband was an abusive alcoholic. I grew up being abused in nearly every sense of the word. By multiple relatives. Which all added up and lead to what would be some of the darkest, but most influential years of my life. I wouldn't suggest anyone else learn about who they are the same way. But, I will say I don't regret all the shit that happened. Because, it made me who I am today. And led me to my wife, and two sons.

So, if anyone is actually interested in this fire away. I will try to respond as quickly as I can. But, if I see something shiny I may get distracted for just a minute.

Edit: Thanks for asking questions! I'm going to bed now. But, if anyone else happens across this and wants to ask something go ahead! I'll be back on tomorrow after work. Some time around 3pm Central or a little later. Whether anyone else has asked something or not. Because, I'm a Voat addict now. I guess it's decent substitution.
By Request: IAMA father of two who was homeless from ages 16 to 20, I was addicted to methamphetamine during that time, and a blackout alcoholic. So, go ahead AMA.
How did you end up homeless? Did you decide to stop living with your parents or were there other circumstances?

It wasn't a choice on my part. I was given the boot. My stepdad didn't like me, because I wasn't as easily put down as the rest. After I learned to stand up for myself and my mom things didn't work too well in the house. At first my mom was with me, but she ended up going back home when he asked and I was left. She didn't do it because she didn't care about me. Just to be clear. But, she grew up being beaten and everything else too. And she got to a point where she couldn't deal with life without that constant darkness there. It's what she knew best, I guess.

The story on that is pretty simple really. They had been fighting, more than usual, for weeks. Screaming and cussing at each other. I got up and was trying to get ready for school. And it just kept getting worse and worse. Finally I came out of the bathroom, and said, "You guys are the adults here, why don't you just talk?". And, my stepdad said something along the lines of "I'm going to beat your fucking ass."

My mom touched his shoulder and he took a swing at her. And when he realized what he did in front of me, he turned around and saw me running to them. That's when I was no longer welcome in my own home. I really wasn't before, but I was tolerated at least. And to back up the point he started getting his gun and stuff, so my mom told me not to worry about it. We would both leave. So, we packed what we could and left. A couple months into living at an RV park she went back. And, I was left living out of my little '95 Toyota Corolla. Which I was really lucky to make it out with. Even if I didn't always have it to sleep in.
Did you at least get a chance to beat his ass before you got kicked out? Reading about your stepdad doing that to your mom got my blood boiling.

Not that day. I wanted to murder him. I've never been that enraged in my life. But, a year later he finally followed through and took a swing. I looked him in the eyes and said (in as cool a voice as a homeless kid could pull off), "You just fucked up." and got my revenge. In the middle of a busy store. And when the crowd finally got me off of him they jumped on him, and slammed him into a wall. They were all super nice to me, and made sure I had everything and let me go. They made sure he stayed there for awhile after I left, I guess.

He went to the police, and they came to talk to me. But, they just told me it was whatever. They weren't going to do anything. But, they had some back story on us too. So that helped a lot.

You say you were homeless until the age of twenty. What happened at that point? How did you get back on your feet?

Also, what made you want to get sober and how did you do it?

A series of events that led up to me being able to stay with a friend I hadn't seen since 4th grade. He moved back to town, and I was just kind of stumbling around drunk on the square and ran into him. He had me move in for a couple months. I got a job and met my wife that same summer. And I didn't want to be a bum anymore. I felt disgusting, and had for a long time. But, I didn't just want to lay in the shit and feel bad for myself anymore. So, I saved up some money and moved into an old farm house that was falling apart, with rent that was way too high for what it was, and he moved back out of state. My wife and I got married. And, I just started working my ass off. I had started trying to cut back on the alcohol when we found out she was pregnant. That's when I emptied the last bottle in the house, and started trying to quit. I had already wanted to. It was getting old, and I couldn't remember a lot of stuff because I was too drunk when it happened. But, my son was the final push for sobriety.

As far as getting back on my feet... it was a lot of hard work. Horrible manual labor jobs, and having bosses that would only pay you for 30 hours of your 50 hour work week, and keep your holiday pay. We still aren't in a great spot financially, but we keep moving forward and up. And we can at least keep food in out bellies, and a roof over our heads. And, even though I still work a terrible manual labor job I have nice benefits, and get paid for all the hours I work now. So that's a plus too.

But, without my wife, and the realization I going to be father. Things wouldn't have ended up this pretty. I was really selfdestructive, and still find myself trying to go back to those old habbits some times. They saved me from that mentality and from the alcohol. Seeing myself in the mirror while sober was a good way to decide to quit meth. At that point I was still alone, so the only way I'd stop is if I decided to. When you are on it you don't realize what you are like. You don't see the same person everyone else does when you look in the mirror. You're hot shit. You're unstoppable. You don't see the you that spends two hours digging through and organizing the $5 movie bin at walmart and chewing on your own tongue.

At that time when you were being abused, and there was no help, what should people do so they can find and help someone in that situation?

Would mobile phones with video cameras have changed things for you?

Pay attention. People will show you when they are being abused. You'll notice the hints, you just have to trust your gut on it, because most likely they won't tell you flat out. Not while its happening. But, you really have to be tactful and very careful about how you approach them and the situation. People can get really defensive and angry when they are approached about being abused. A solid piece of advice is don't be like the people in my life. If a child comes to you and directly tells you something like that. Take it serious. Look into it. Most small children will not intentionally lie about things like that. And if they do they had to learn it from somewhere. But, even if their story isn't perfectly solid and true, it doesn't mean they are just telling lies. It's how they understand and interpret what is happening.

To anyone who may read this answer that is being abused. Don't be afraid. You are better than what you are being put through, and you deserve more. Stand up and tell someone. It can be scary as fuck, but you have to do it. And once you do you will feel a relief and a freedom you've not been able to imagine in a long time. It will take some time to recover from what happened/is happening, but you can do it and you deserve so much more.

A phone with a camera wouldn't have helped me any. But, I'm odd like that, and very stubborn. I've always been very set in that idea that I have to rely on myself for everything. So, after I had family and friends call me a liar, at 4, I refused to ask for help again. I chose to get angry and to get strong. I knew at that point that I was alone and couldn't trust anyone else to be there for me. That's a weird realization to have when you are about to go into Kindergarten.

I think now though phones do help. You can record video or audio, and take pictures of the damage. And there are apps you can use to secretly alert the right people when you are a victim of domestic abuse. Just don't be stubborn and think you have to deal with it alone like I did.
How is substance use different in reality compared to what you hear from mainstream non-user sources?

People seem to think drugs and alcohol make you do thing. Drugs don't break into your house, hold your wife at gun point and say the will kill her if you don't do what they want.

Drugs help lower your inhibitions but they don't make you do anything. The decisions you make are your own. You still have the final say, and you still have to deal with the consequences. Nobody else can say drugs did it and neither can you. You made the choices. The drugs were a factor but that is the end of their decision making ability.

Yeah you do things you don't remember. But you made the decisions that led up to that.

But, that being said. Substance abuse is a weird situation. You aren't really your normal self anymore. There are a lot of little factors that build to that point. And there is a lot of underlying emotional and mental damage there before you wind up shooting something into your veins. Drug abuse is a cry for help. Even though you don't realize while your drinking or shooting up. You're self medicating trying to fix, or hide from what's broken. Trying to fix the loneliness, or hide from that feeling of failure, or trying to fill a hole in your heart. Because you don't know how to cope with it at the time.

Bad coping skills lead to some really rough life lessons. I wish there was more emphasis on showing people how to deal with the shit in life. The anger, the hurt, the loneliness, then we would see fewer people abusing substances like that. It wouldn't stop the problem. But it would help. When you know what the right tool is you won't try to create one with meth or whiskey.

Regarding the opiate tolerance reducer - it's ultra low dose naltrexone. regular dose naltrexone blocks all the opiate channels and is used by former addicts to make opiates have zero effect. However, ultra low dose of the same drug on blocks the kappa receptor which is responsible for addiction and tolerance. The dose is about 60ug per 1ml, so as you can tell very small. Regular naltrexone is used also to treat alcohol and nicotine addiction but it doesn't work for everyone, still it's not a bad idea to give it a try when trying to stop using those substances. ultra low dose naltrexone is dose dependent, light users need only a few drops, while heavy ones might need significantly more. It works much more efficiently if taken continuously over the course of several days. A dose lasts about 4-5 hrs. Here's some more info
